This report studies low-bit adaptation of Vision Transformers under the joint constraints of limited downstream data, restricted trainable parameters, and severe quantization noise. The project develops Quantized Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (QPEFT), a fake-quantization-based adaptation framework that keeps most pretrained
backbone parameters frozen while jointly optimizing Low-Rank Adaptation (

) modules, the task classification head, and selected quantization-related parameters. The implementation targets attention and feed-forward linear projections, incorporates low-bit weight and activation quantizers, and uses adaptive activation treatment for post-

and post-GELU tensors. To avoid an abrupt transition from full-precision adaptation to low-bit simulation, the framework introduces Stochastic Element-wise Exposure to Quantization (SEEQ), which progressively exposes tensor elements to dequantized low-bit values during training. Empirical evaluation is conducted with

-L/16 backbones on VTAB-style classification tasks, together with comparisons against post-training quantization and QAT-style baselines, supplementary full-image classification results, and ablations on shift and stochastic exposure scheduling. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) can often recover more accuracy because the model is exposed to quantization effects during training before deployment. However, QAT introduces its own optimization difficulties. Low-bit QAT relies on straight-through gradient approximations to handle non-differentiable rounding operations, and existing work shows that quantized weights may oscillate between adjacent quantization grid points during training [22]. 2.1 Vision Transformers and Efficient Visual Adaptation

Transformer architectures were first established as sequence models built around self-attention, where contextual relationships are modeled through learned interactions among tokens rather than through recurrence or fixed convolutional locality [1]. Vision Transformer (
) transferred this formulation to images by representing an image as a sequence of patch tokens and processing the sequence with Transformer encoder blocks [2]. This shift was important not

only because it challenged the dominance of convolutional neural networks in visual recognition, but also because it made visual modeling increasingly dependent on large linear projections, attention maps, normalization layers, and token-wise feed-forward networks. These components are central to the quantization problem studied in this project, since their numerical distributions and interactions differ from those in conventional convolutional backbones.

These developments indicate that efficient visual adaptation is not only a matter of reducing parameters. 2.3 Quantization-Aware Training for Low-Bit Vision Transformers

Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) addresses a different weakness of PTQ by exposing the model to quantization effects during training or fine-tuning. Classical integer-oriented quantization work established how fake quantization during training can prepare models for lower-precision inference [6]. Learned Step Size Quantization (LSQ) made the quantization step size itself learnable, which is closely related to the learnable quantization parameters used in this project [7]. In principle, QAT provides a stronger mechanism than PTQ because the model can adapt to quantization noise through gradient-based optimization. In practice, this advantage comes with higher training
, sensitivity to hyperparameters, and potential instability in low-bit regimes.

is a representative QAT-oriented study for low-bit Vision Transformers [20]. It identifies information distortion in the self-attention map as a major source of performance degradation and introduces information rectification and distribution-guided distillation to preserve quantized attention behavior. This line of work is valuable for QPEFT because it confirms that attention is not a passive victim of quantization, but a central site where low-bit
errors can reshape model behavior. Nevertheless, Q-
is designed around a fully quantized training pipeline with specialized distillation and rectification. The present project instead asks whether a mostly frozen
can be adapted through a small number of trainable parameters while still being exposed to quantization effects.

A second QAT issue is oscillation. General oscillation-aware QAT work shows that quantized weights can move between adjacent grid points during simulated quantization, leading to unstable optimization and degraded inference behavior [22]. OFQ extends this concern to low-bit

and observes that learnable scaling factors may aggravate weight oscillation, while query and key projections in self-attention can interact in ways that intensify instability [21]. This is directly relevant to QPEFT because the current implementation uses learnable quantization-related parameters and adapts attention projections through

. The literature therefore supports a careful claim boundary. QPEFT can be described as quantization-aware parameter-efficient fine-tuning, but it should not be described as conventional full-model QAT.

The QAT literature highlights a trade-off that motivates the hybrid positioning of this project. PTQ is efficient but can be too rigid when downstream adaptation is required. Full QAT is adaptive but expensive and potentially unstable under ultra-low precision. A fake-QAT-style PEFT approach offers an intermediate path. It incorporates quantization effects during downstream optimization, as QAT does, but restricts trainable capacity mainly to adapters, the task head, and selected quantization-related parameters. This is why QPEFT is more accurately positioned as quantization-aware parameter-efficient adaptation rather than as either standard PTQ or full-model QAT.

2.5 Research Gap and Positioning of This Project

The related work reveals a clear separation among three research streams. ViT research provides strong transferable visual backbones but also exposes deployment cost and token-interaction sensitivity. PTQ research provides efficient low-data quantization but remains limited when quantization must be combined with downstream adaptation. QAT research exposes quantization effects during optimization but can be computationally heavy and unstable at very low bit-widths. PEFT research reduces trainable parameters but does not by itself solve low-bit numerical mismatch. These observations are summarized in Table 2.

Model quantization maps floating-point weights or activations to a finite set of low-bit values. In a uniform quantizer, a real-valued tensor x is scaled, shifted by a zero point, rounded to the nearest representable integer level, clipped to the valid integer range, and then dequantized back to the floating-point domain for simulated training. Quantized Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (QPEFT) is the proposed framework of this report. It combines

The baseline protocol separates method families rather than forcing them into a single identical training recipe. Full-precision LoRA provides an adaptation reference. PTQ baselines quantify the behaviour of calibration or reconstruction-oriented quantization methods. QAT-style baselines examine low-bit optimization without the same LoRA-based adaptation path. QPEFT is then evaluated as a hybrid quantization-aware adaptation strategy in which most backbone weights remain frozen while LoRA modules, the task head, and selected quantization-related parameters are optimized.

The ablation protocol focuses on two implementation-level factors that are directly relevant to ViT activation quantization. The first is a post-GELU shift treatment, which is motivated by the asymmetric distribution of GELU activations. The second is the stochastic exposure schedule, controlled by the drop epoch parameter, which determines how quickly the model is exposed to quantized values during training. Together, these ablations test whether QPEFT benefits from distribution-aware activation handling and gradual exposure to low-bit perturbations.

The current method should therefore be described as quantization-aware parameter-efficient fine-tuning, or as a fake-QAT-style QPEFT framework for

adaptation. It is closer to QAT than PTQ because quantization effects are included during downstream optimization, but it remains parameter-efficient because the pre-trained backbone is mostly frozen. This classification is used consistently throughout the report to avoid overstating the method as either standard PTQ or conventional full-model QAT.

The report should also maintain a clear distinction between simulated quantization and deployable integer inference. Fake quantization is sufficient for studying optimization stability and low-bit adaptation behavior, but it does not by itself prove speedup, power reduction, or hardware deployment readiness. Such claims require an exported integer model and controlled measurement on a target hardware platform [23].

This section reports the evaluation protocol and empirical results for Quantized Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (QPEFT) on Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones. The evaluation follows a classification-oriented VTAB-style setting [5] and compares QPEFT with representative Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) methods, QAT-style baselines, supplementary full-image classification runs, and targeted ablations. TensorBoard logs are used as case-study diagnostics for training trajectory and gradient behavior rather than as a replacement for the main tabular results.

The protocol is organized to separate broad task-level evaluation from diagnostic analysis. The main results report ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 performance using Natural, Specialized, and Structured task groups. The PTQ comparison includes AdaLog [16], RepQ-ViT [15], PTQ4ViT [14], and QDrop [11] where matched settings are available. The QAT-style baselines and supplementary CIFAR, Food101, and SVHN results provide additional reference points, while the ablation study isolates the effects of post-GELU shift and stochastic exposure scheduling.

All accuracy values in this chapter are reported as percentages. The VTAB-style tasks are grouped into Natural, Specialized, and Structured task families. Group Avg denotes the unweighted mean of the three group averages, while Tot. Avg denotes the direct average over the 19 task accuracies. Tot. Avg is used as the primary summary metric when it is available, because the three task groups contain different numbers of datasets.

Across both backbones, Structured tasks remain persistently more difficult than Natural and Specialized tasks. This is an important observation because it prevents the discussion from reducing the project to a single average number. Natural tasks often rely heavily on transferred visual appearance features, and Specialized tasks can benefit from strong pretrained representation when the domain shift is manageable. Structured tasks, by contrast, include tasks that require geometric sensitivity, counting, spatial reasoning, or controlled visual relation understanding. These tasks are likely more vulnerable to small perturbations in token representation, attention maps, and intermediate activation distributions. Low-bit quantization can distort precisely those subtle relational cues, so the weaker Structured results are not an incidental failure. 5.2 Relation to PTQ, QAT, and PEFT Baselines

The comparison with Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) baselines leads to a nuanced conclusion. Well-designed PTQ methods remain competitive in some 4-bit settings. At the same time, several PTQ baselines degrade sharply at 3-bit precision, while QPEFT retains
stronger average accuracy by combining low-bit simulation with trainable LoRA-based adaptation.

The advantage of QPEFT becomes clearer when the bit-width is reduced or when the backbone is more sensitive to direct post-training quantization. In the PTQ comparison, ViT-B/16 3-bit QPEFT reaches 69.95 Tot. Avg, while the best matched PTQ result reported in Section 4 is QDrop at 61.72. At 4-bit precision, AdaLog remains strong on ViT-B/16 with 70.16 Tot. Avg, but QPEFT reaches 71.21 under the same backbone family.
This pattern is plausible from the perspective of

. PTQ methods address these issues through quantizer design, scale reparameterization, activation-specific transforms, or reconstruction objectives. QPEFT takes a different route: it allows a small set of trainable adaptation and quantization parameters to respond to the simulated quantization noise during task adaptation. This does not make PTQ obsolete. It means that, in the evaluation record, the adaptation capacity introduced by
particularly helpful when the low-bit constraint is too strong for calibration-style correction alone.
The Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) comparison leads to a different conclusion. The QAT-style baselines sheet in Section 4 reports direct QAT-style optimization without
-style adaptation, with Tot. Avg values of 52.79 for 3-bit and 57.83 for 4-bit. These baselines are much lower than the corresponding

-B/16 QPEFT results of 69.95 and 71.21. The interpretation should be limited to this project setting. It does not prove that QPEFT universally dominates all QAT methods, because modern full-model QAT methods may use different schedules, losses, initialization strategies, distillation objectives, or oscillation-control mechanisms. What the sheet does show is that directly applying quantization-aware optimization without a parameter-efficient adaptation path is less stable under the present data, model, and training configuration.
This result is important for the method claim because QPEFT is not a standard full-model QAT method. The backbone is mostly frozen, while
parameters, the classification head, and selected quantization-related parameters are trained. This design gives the model enough flexibility to compensate for

result matrix supports this positioning: it benefits from including quantization effects during optimization, while also benefiting from the regularization and efficiency of a restricted trainable parameter set.
The relationship to Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) baselines is also nuanced. The FP32

rows establish the upper reference for parameter-efficient adaptation without low-bit constraints, and QPEFT should be judged by how much of that reference it preserves after quantization. The results indicate that the gap is small for

The ablation evidence in Section 4 is useful because it links the observed performance to specific empirical design factors. The shift ablation compares a no-shift setting with a post-GELU shift setting. The reported Tot. Avg increases from 64.56 to 69.84 when the constant post-GELU shift is used. This does not, by itself, prove a complete causal theory, but it strongly suggests that post-GELU activation handling is an important part of the method's stability. It also matches the broader problem structure of
quantization, where post-GELU activations can be asymmetric and difficult to approximate with a simple low-bit grid.

The most direct interpretation is that the shift improves the alignment between the activation distribution and the adaptive activation quantizer. GELU produces negative values in a narrow interval and positive values with a broader range. Under low-bit quantization, a poorly aligned quantization grid can waste representational levels or introduce uneven clipping and rounding errors. A constant shift can make the distribution more compatible with the quantizer, allowing the same bit budget to represent useful activation regions more effectively. This mechanism is especially relevant for the MLP branch, where post-GELU tensors feed into the second linear layer and can propagate quantization error through subsequent residual computations.

The shift result is consistent with the known difficulty of quantizing asymmetric post-GELU activations. It supports treating post-GELU activation handling as an important design factor in low-bit QPEFT.

parameters chase unstable quantization noise. Later in training, increasing exposure to dequantized low-bit values improves alignment between the trained adaptation path and the quantized evaluation

The exposure-schedule ablation suggests that gradually exposing the model to quantized values is useful, but the schedule must be tuned. Very early exposure can destabilize adaptation, while overly delayed exposure reduces the opportunity to adapt to the low-bit forward path.

The reliability of the findings is stronger than in the earlier project stage because the evaluation now covers multiple levels: VTAB-style results for ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16, multiple bit-widths, PTQ comparisons, QAT-style baselines, supplementary full-image classification results, ablations, and TensorBoard diagnostics.

The evaluation protocol separates task-level accuracy from optimization diagnostics. The VTAB-style results are the primary basis for classification-oriented downstream adaptation. The PTQ and QAT-style comparisons provide baseline context, while the CIFAR training curves explain optimization behavior at a finer level.

Reproducibility is supported by the implementation structure described in the Methods and Results sections. The training entry, configuration choices, bit-width settings, LoRA injection targets, quantization settings, and recorded results form a traceable chain from implementation
to reported numbers. This is sufficient for a final-year engineering report, although a stronger research artifact would release all scripts, logs, and checkpoints in a curated repository.

The TensorBoard diagnostics add depth but not breadth. They provide deeper analysis only for the CIFAR case study, including the training trajectory and selected gradient behaviours for LoRA and quantizer-related parameters.

The main limitation is that the evaluation appears to rely on limited seed coverage. Single-seed or narrow-seed results are useful for establishing feasibility, but they cannot fully characterize variance. A stronger validation would repeat key ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 configurations across multiple random seeds and report means and standard deviations.

There are also data integrity risks when many task-wise results are aggregated manually. The safest interpretation is to treat the reported values as a coherent experimental summary that still benefits from final cross-checking against raw logs and independent reruns.

Baseline fairness is another constraint. PTQ, QAT, and QPEFT methods have different assumptions, trainable parameter sets, calibration requirements, and hyperparameter sensitivities. A perfectly fair comparison would require method-specific tuning budgets and matched data protocols. The current comparison is still meaningful because it reflects the project setting and evaluation matrix, but it should not be presented as a universal ranking of all PTQ, QAT, and PEFT methods. The absence of real integer runtime deployment is a related limitation. The reported results are based on fake quantization and simulated low-bit
, so they support accuracy retention under quantization simulation rather than measured speed, latency, memory bandwidth, or energy gains on integer hardware.

The evaluation combines multiple sources of information, including task-level accuracy tables, supplementary classification results, ablations, and diagnostic training logs. This combination is appropriate for an engineering final report, but future work should consolidate these records into a single reproducible evaluation pipeline.

Two implementation-related limitations remain. First, the shift and exposure-schedule factors should be documented more explicitly in code-level terms. Second, the study focuses on fake quantization and does not yet include integer export or runtime benchmarking.
This project investigated how ultra-low-bit Vision Transformer (

) adaptation can be made more stable when the available downstream data and trainable parameter budget are both constrained. The central problem was not simply to quantize a pretrained model after training, nor to perform conventional full-model Quantization-Aware Training (QAT). Instead, the project asked whether quantization and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) can be coupled so that the adaptation path learns under the same low-bit numerical perturbations that will be present during evaluation.
The resulting framework, Quantized Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (QPEFT), was developed as a fake-QAT-style adaptation pipeline for
models. The implemented version keeps most of the pretrained backbone frozen, injects Low-Rank Adaptation (

) modules into selected attention and multilayer perceptron projections, and jointly optimizes the trainable adapters, the classification head, and selected quantization-related parameters. This design gives the model a limited but targeted adaptation space, rather than relying on either static post-training calibration or expensive full-backbone retraining.

A key methodological component is Stochastic Element-wise Exposure to Quantization (SEEQ). SEEQ expresses the training-time idea that individual tensor elements can be exposed either to their continuous full-precision values or to their dequantized low-bit counterparts. In practical terms, this prevents the model from being forced into the full low-bit regime at the beginning of optimization. It also gives the

path and learnable quantization parameters an opportunity to absorb quantization noise progressively. The method therefore treats quantization as part of downstream adaptation, rather than as an afterthought applied after the adapter has already been learned.

The experimental results support the main claim within the evaluated configurations. The VTAB-style results show that LoRA-based QPEFT preserves competitive performance under 3-bit and 4-bit fake quantization for both ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16. In the reported ViT-B/16 setting, the 3-bit and 4-bit QPEFT rows reach Tot. Avg values of 69.95 and 71.21. In the ViT-L/16 setting, the corresponding values are 72.99 and 73.68.

The comparison with Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) baselines leads to a nuanced conclusion. Well-designed PTQ methods remain competitive in some 4-bit settings. At the same time, several PTQ baselines degrade sharply at 3-bit precision, while QPEFT retains
stronger average accuracy by combining low-bit simulation with trainable LoRA-based adaptation.

The QAT-style baseline comparison also clarifies the contribution of PEFT. Direct low-bit optimization without LoRA-style adaptation is less stable than the corresponding QPEFT configurations in the evaluated setting. This does not imply that QPEFT universally dominates all QAT algorithms, but it supports the value of combining quantization-aware training dynamics with parameter-efficient downstream adaptation.

The ablation study further supports the design rationale. The shift result suggests that post-GELU activation handling is important, and the exposure-schedule result suggests that gradual quantization exposure improves stability when compared with poorly timed exposure schedules.
Overall, the project demonstrates a coherent and reproducible route for studying low-bit
-based PEFT, learnable quantization parameters, adaptive activation quantization, and progressive stochastic exposure. The most important conclusion is that low-bit

adaptation benefits from being optimized under the quantized numerical condition, but it does not necessarily require updating the entire backbone. This provides a practical middle ground between efficient PTQ and costly full-model QAT, while keeping the claims
to fake quantization, classification-oriented VTAB-style evaluation, and the available project evidence.

The current results are sufficient to justify QPEFT as a promising framework for low-bit ViT adaptation, but several extensions are needed before the method can be treated as a general deployment solution. The following directions extend the project from a validated final-year study toward a stronger research artifact.

• Broader and cleaner validation. The first priority is to repeat the key ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 configurations across multiple random seeds and to verify task-level results against raw logs. This would allow the reportable results to move from single-run trends to mean and variance estimates.
. A natural next step is to test whether QPEFT remains stable on object detection and semantic segmentation, where spatial localization, token-level detail, and feature quantization can
be more fragile than image-level classification. These experiments should be positioned as validation of generality, not as
consequences of the current VTAB results.
backbones and a more systematic study of sensitive modules. Mixed-precision protection for

, post-GELU activations, or attention projections may help identify where full low-bit quantization is unnecessary or harmful. This direction is especially relevant because current results suggest that model scale and activation treatment both influence low-bit retention.

• Stronger ablation and PEFT coverage. The shift and drop_epc factors should be documented at implementation level and then evaluated with a broader ablation protocol. Beyond LoRA, future work could compare alternative PEFT variants such as adapters, selective tuning, or weight-decomposed low-rank adaptation.
The present project studies fake quantization and accuracy retention. A deployment-oriented extension should export
low-bit or integer-compatible models, measure latency, memory use, and energy on a defined hardware target, and separate simulated compression from actual runtime benefit.
This would turn QPEFT from an optimization study into a more complete compression and deployment pipeline.
